summary: This tutorial-style video is a landscape photography processing guide focusing on a New Zealand rainforest scene. The presenter outlines a philosophy-heavy workflow (artistic philosophy, compositional rules, and how to move the eye through a frame), then demonstrates a zone-based approach to raw and Photoshop processing. Core moves include extracting shadow detail, controlling global exposure and blacks, applying selective saturation and color adjustments, and building depth via diffuse light, fog, and layer separation. Distinctive techniques cover perspective corrections (perspective warp and puppet warp), multiple-stage masking and history-based editing, creation of light beams through blur and clone-paint workflows, aggressive sky work with auto HDR-like tonemapping and manual sky blending, and careful final cropping to emphasize a focal peak. The session also emphasizes avoiding over-precise selections for natural blending, maintaining depth by separating layers, and plotting a directional light path to guide the eye to the light source and subject. The narrative touches on field considerations (Milford/Fiordland context) and on how to judge when to crop or warp, and when to preserve a scene’s natural relationships between foreground, middle ground, and background.

sections.title: Intro to artistic philosophy and base tools
sections.description: The narrator introduces the process and points to a companion ‘Artistic Philosophy’ video and a compositional rules sheet, emphasizing the 'why' behind processing and how it affects depth, movement of the eye, and scene simplification.

sections.title: Composition, framing, and the rule of six
sections.description: Discussion of compositional structure and how to crop to enhance eye flow. The speaker advocates evaluating the frame as six parts, removing distracting areas, and ensuring all zones contribute to the overall flow.

sections.title: Initial RAW processing strategy (shadow detail, exposure, dehaze)
sections.description: First processing pass focuses on extracting shadow detail, suppressing overall exposure, and applying light dehaze to set a baseline that preserves mood while keeping highlights controlled.

sections.title: Photoshop workflow setup and historical states
sections.description: The workflow describes enabling thousands of history states for recording, then using Photoshop to adjust the form of the image (warp/crop) before deeper processing.

sections.title: Foreground/background separation and initial color work
sections.description: A cornerstone segment about breaking the image into zones so foreground and background can be optimized separately. Includes lowering the exposure to foreground whites and using selective color to push ferns forward without altering the background.

sections.title: Light diffusion behind trunks and overall atmosphere
sections.description: Techniques to diffuse light behind tree trunks, brighten/mist the mid-ground, and balance blacks/whites to create separation and depth, with discussion of color warmth and selective diffusion for background enhancement.

sections.title: Beams creation and multi-layer separation
sections.description: An in-depth walkthrough of creating light beams using Gaussian blur, clone-painting from a blurred layer, and meticulous hard/soft brush work to separate beams from surrounding clouds, including cautions about edge control and alignment.

sections.title: HDR-like tonemapping, sky work, and final balance
sections.description: Discussion of leveraging HDR-like tonemapping and color grade to bring out clouds and sky shapes, including manual sky blending between shots and final color balancing to ensure consistent tonality and mood.

sections.title: Final composition choices, cropping, and lens-warp considerations
sections.description: The closing segments cover final cropping choices to emphasize lenticular clouds and peak composition, discussion of perspective warp vs puppet warp for controlling distortion, and final color decisions (blues versus golds, tonal shifts, and edge softening) before concluding the session.
